newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU believes it has firm hand on barley market -ONI.
newsitem.headline: EU believes it has firm hand on barley market -ONI.

text.p: The European Union has adopted a tough line on the pricing of barley sold to Saudi Arabia but will eventually cover Europe's full share of the deal, the head of France's cereals office predicted on Wednesday.
ONIC director general Alain Moulinier said traders and the Commission were involved in a ritual "game" over the value of export subsidies but he was confident this would be resolved.
"The grain will eventually go out," he told a news conference on ONIC's latest supply/demand figures.
Saudi Arabia in January bought 1.2 million tonnes of optional-origin barley for February and March delivery.
"The European Commission thinks we are in a position of force on this market and people should align themselves to our prices," Moulinier said.
"It is always rather a complicated game," he added.
But he suggested the lack of obvious alternative suppliers for the time being seemed to show the Commission was right.
"Objectively, there are not a lot of other supplies around," he said.
Moulinier said the recent sale of 1.2 million tonnes of barley was behind ONIC's decision to raise its export estimate to non-EU countries by 400,000 tonnes to 1.5 million tonnes.
EU officials say they expected to supply around 800,000 tonnes of the total barley deal, with about 300-400,000 tonnes left to be done.
But so far the Commission has been wary of granting the highest bids for export refunds at its weekly tender.
Its latest export award of 26,000 tonnes valued its barley around $133 per tonne, traders said.
If the EU does grant the full volume which its exporters hope to sell, France still has to face extra competition inside Europe as a supplier of barley this year.

ONIC officials noted that Spain, with a big crop last year, is now for the first time competitive on the world barley market by using ordinary EU export subsidies. Previously it had needed extra help in the form of a special export tender.
Traders say about 75,000 tonnes of recent barley export licences are for use in Spanish ports that can take large ships.

For Spain, the prospect of a Saudi outlet is a bonus -- past outbreaks of swine fever have prevented it selling barley to many countries that produce pork. Moslem Saudi Arabia, where pork is taboo, has no such worries about buying the grain, French officials said.
